⏺ How TCP Congestion Control Works

  When two computers exchange data over the internet, the path between them crosses many routers and links, each with limited capacity. If every sender transmitted as fast as it could, router queues
  would overflow, packets would be dropped, and senders would retransmit them, which adds even more traffic. This feedback loop is called congestion collapse. It actually happened on the early
  internet in the mid-1980s, when throughput on some links fell by a factor of a thousand. TCP congestion control was introduced, largely through Van Jacobson's work in 1988, to keep this from
  happening. It lets each sender find out how much the network can carry and adjust its sending rate to match.

  The central idea is the congestion window, usually written cwnd. TCP already has a receive window, which keeps the sender from overwhelming the receiver. The congestion window keeps the sender from
  overwhelming the network. At any moment, a sender may have no more than the smaller of these two windows' worth of unacknowledged data in flight. The receiver states its window directly, but no one
  reports the network's capacity. The sender has to infer it, mostly from packet loss and, in newer algorithms, from changes in delay.

  Classic TCP congestion control, as found in TCP Reno and its descendants, has several cooperating mechanisms:

  - Slow start: A new connection starts with a small window, historically one to four segments and now commonly ten. Every acknowledgment (ACK) received grows the window by one segment, so the window
    roughly doubles every round-trip time. Despite its name, this growth is exponential. It lets a connection quickly discover roughly how much bandwidth is available.
  -
